patches.title: new and make with non-type arguments
patches.origin: treebank; found by the first top-500 module-proxy sweep

evidence.repro:
package a

func f() {
	_ = new("hello")
	_ = new(int32(1000))
	var make func(int) *X
	_ = make(n - 1)
}
evidence.diagnosis: call_expression special-cases the literal tokens 'new' and 'make' and routes them to special_argument_list, whose first element was strictly $._type. But `new` and `make` are PREDECLARED IDENTIFIERS in Go, not keywords, and two separate things follow from that. (1) Go 1.26 added new(expr) — `new(x)` returns a pointer to a copy of x — so the first argument of a real builtin `new` call is now often an expression: a string literal, a conversion, a dereference. Verified against the toolchain: a module with `go 1.26` compiles and runs `new("hello")` and `new(int32(1000))`. (2) Because they are ordinary identifiers, user code can shadow them; k8s.io/kube-openapi vendors a test declaring `var make func(int) *X` and calling `make(n - 1)`. Both shapes reached special_argument_list and had no path. The fix widens that first element to choice($._type, prec.dynamic(-2, $._expression)). The dynamic precedence is the whole subtlety: without it, a BARE IDENTIFIER argument resolves to the expression reading and `new(int)` regresses from (type_identifier) to (identifier) — a tree-shape change every consumer query would feel. At -2 the expression branch loses to the type branch (which carries prec.dynamic(-1) on _type_identifier inside _simple_type), so every pre-existing shape is preserved and only genuinely-non-type arguments take the new path. Verified node by node: make([]int,3) -> slice_type, make(map[string]int) -> map_type, make(chan int,1) -> channel_type, new(int) -> type_identifier, new(struct{A int}) -> struct_type, all unchanged; new("hello") -> interpreted_string_literal and new(int32(1000)) -> call_expression are new.
evidence.evidence_note: One line of grammar.js closes all 6 clusters and all 17 gap files, and the 67 upstream corpus tests plus the new one all pass. The 17 files were 15 Go-1.26 new(expr) uses across k8s.io/kubernetes and k8s.io/apiserver and 2 shadowed-builtin calls in k8s.io/kube-openapi.
evidence.upstream_status: not yet reported upstream; the patch applies directly to the pinned sha. Upstream v0.25.0 predates Go 1.26, so the new(expr) half is upstream falling behind the language rather than a mistake — exactly the case treebank exists for.

generate_cli_note: same pin as the other grammars: tree-sitter-cli 0.26.x ships broken Unicode identifier tables (see treebank-rust ledger). Measured here: 0.25.10 regenerates upstream's committed src/parser.c byte for byte except the `@generated by tree-sitter v0.25.8` version comment, so the pin costs nothing against what upstream shipped.
external_scanner: none — tree-sitter-go is pure grammar.js, so every fix here is a declarative grammar.js change routed to a mid-tier model, never a scanner.c state-machine job. This is also why Go's automatic semicolon insertion is not modelled; see grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.

corpus.source: The Go module proxy: proxy.golang.org/<module>/@v/<version>.zip, one immutable zip per version. There is no tarball registry for Go and this is a cleaner source than any already wired up — content-addressed, notarised by the checksum database, never re-uploaded or deleted, and one URL per version rather than a wheel-vs-sdist choice (PyPI), a conventionally-named sources jar that may not exist (Maven), or three decompressors (Debian). Versions are resolved from the proxy's @latest at fetch time.
corpus.source_note: Module paths and versions are CASE-ENCODED on the proxy: every uppercase letter becomes '!' plus its lowercase, so the proxy can serve from case-insensitive filesystems. Measured: github.com/BurntSushi/toml 404s unencoded and 200s as github.com/!burnt!sushi/toml. A module zip also prefixes every entry with <module>@<version>/, which is THREE path components for github.com/spf13/cobra@v1.10.2/ — the first zip treebank has met that needs stripping at all, and the reason Lang::archive_strip exists.
corpus.ranking: ecosyste.ms, registry proxy.golang.org, sorted by dependent_repos_count — the same source and the same metric java uses
corpus.ranking_note: Go publishes no download counts anywhere. The module proxy deliberately does not release its logs; pkg.go.dev's 'known importers' listing is capped (15 for github.com/stretchr/testify, measured, against a real dependent count in the tens of thousands); and deps.dev's documented API states dependent counts cover 'npm, Cargo, Maven and PyPI' — Go is absent and the endpoint 404s. So this is a dependency-graph proxy, not traffic, and NOT the same kind of metric as crates.io/npm/PyPI downloads. One quirk is specific to Go: a go.mod records the whole transitive requirement set rather than direct imports, so modules nobody imports directly rank high — github.com/pmezard/go-difflib sits at #2 purely because testify depends on it. Those are still real, widely compiled modules, so the corpus is legitimate; the ranking just should not be read as 'what Go programmers import'.
corpus.files_note: .go only, the single extension tree-sitter-go's tree-sitter.json claims. Excluded by PATH, using go/build's own rule rather than a treebank heuristic: any directory or file whose name begins with '_' or '.', and testdata/ entirely — the go tool ignores all of them, and testdata/ is where a Go project keeps deliberately-broken fixtures. vendor/ is excluded for the reason python excludes _vendor/ and javascript excludes bundles: it is a verbatim copy of other modules, so a failure there is attributed to the wrong package. _test.go files are KEPT; they are ordinary Go compiled by `go test` and carry syntax the rest of a package often does not.
corpus.files_note_evidence: The path filter is doing real work and it was measured rather than assumed. Of 11,619 .go files in the top-100 zips with no filtering at all, the oracle rejects exactly 11 — and all 11 are deliberately-broken fixtures under testdata/ (cmd/fiximports/testdata/src/old.com/bad/bad.go, go/loader/testdata/badpkgdecl.go, and a generics fixture whose error is 'method must have no type parameters'). The filtered corpus has zero rejects.
corpus.build_tags_note: Go needs no treebank_preprocessing, and this is measured rather than assumed. Go build constraints (//go:build) are WHOLE-FILE, never within-file: there is no #if-style branch splitting, so a constrained file is still ordinary Go text and go/parser reads it exactly as written. There is therefore none of the parse-vs-compile divergence that crate exists to absorb. Measured on the top-100 corpus: 1382 of 10486 files carry a constraint, including 164 `//go:build ignore`, 42 windows, 14 solaris and 14 `//go:build go1.27` gated on a toolchain NEWER than the one installed — all 1382 parse. Not one of the corpus's rejected files was excluded by a build tag; every exclusion is by path.
corpus.oracle: tools/go-oracle — go/parser.ParseFile with parser.SkipObjectResolution, the parser the Go toolchain itself runs, driven through the batch stdin_oracle. TWO-VALUED: valid / invalid. It never type-checks, resolves an import or assembles a package, so an unresolved identifier is not an error and each file is judged entirely on its own text. SkipObjectResolution additionally turns off the deprecated ast.Object/ast.Scope graph, which is the one part of ParseFile that tries to link identifiers to declarations — information a single file with no package context does not have.
corpus.oracle_version_note: The toolchain version IS the language version and is load-bearing exactly as generate_cli is. Go 1.26's new(expr) is the live example: it is the feature behind patch 0003, and on go1.25 those same corpus files would be oracle-INVALID and recorded as noise rather than as the grammar gap they are. Bumping it is treated like a patch: full sweep, before/after numbers, ledger entry.
corpus.oracle_verified_per_file: Verified rather than trusted, at 10x the roadmap's evidence: 8144 files (1650 from ten proxy-fetched modules, 6494 from the Go standard library) returned 8144 valid verdicts in their source trees, and the SAME 8144 verdicts after every file was copied into one flat directory with mangled names (f00123.go) and no go.mod — which also strips Go's own _test.go and _linux.go filename semantics. It rejects correctly too: all 7 of go/parser's .src fixtures carrying syntax ERROR markers come back invalid and the 3 without come back valid, and a go/types fixture whose only ERROR is 'overflows int32' is correctly called VALID, because that is a type error and not a syntax error.
corpus.oracle_cost: 0.61 s per 1000 files serial and 0.078 s per 1000 at 16 workers, measured on the full 68006-file / 1558 MB corpus (41.41 s and 5.28 s respectively) — 38 MB/s serial, 295 MB/s parallel. Throughput is flat across every file-size decile, so seconds-per-1000-FILES tracks corpus composition rather than the oracle: the same binary measures 1.39 s/1000 on the top-100 subset, which averages 41 KB/file because of cloud.google.com/go's generated clients, against 22.9 KB across the top 500. The ROADMAP's 1.94 s/1000 is consistent with a fatter corpus still. Firmly Tier A on any of these. The reject path is 0.41 s/1000 serial on files truncated to 60% — 1.5x FASTER than the valid path, like rust's syn, because go/parser bails at the first error instead of recovering.
corpus.packages_note: 500 requested, 500 resolved and fetched, zero skips — the first language where nothing is dropped at the resolve step. Nothing in the module proxy is optional the way an sdist or a sources jar is.
corpus.remaining_gaps_note: None. 68006 of 68006 files parse, and zero files in the corpus are oracle-invalid, so there is no noise either. That is an unusually clean result and the reason is worth stating rather than celebrating: Go's syntax is small, has been stable since 1.18, has no preprocessor and no dialects, and the path filter removes the testdata/ trees where the invalid files live. The negative corpus, not the sweep, is where this grammar's real risk sits.
corpus.oracle_unreadable_note: An unreadable file is NOT an invalid file, and the oracle exits non-zero rather than emitting a verdict for one. The principle is borrowed from exec_oracle.rs, which reasons it out for the fork-per-file oracles: a broken oracle must fail loudly, never quietly agree with us. It is not hypothetical here. validate() is only ever called on files the grammar already failed, and an invalid verdict records the file as corpus NOISE — so a mistyped corpus root would make every path unreadable, every grammar failure noise, gap_files zero, and the sweep would report a flawless grammar. The read is therefore separate from the parse and an I/O error is fatal with the path on stderr.
corpus.oracle_concurrency: Parallel with goroutines inside the single batch process, NOT one process per file. exec_oracle.rs exists for reference parsers with no batch mode (php -l, luac -p, bash -n) and routing Go through it would be a regression — it would pay process startup 68006 times to avoid a cost go-oracle does not have. The lesson that did transfer is that this work is embarrassingly parallel, so it is applied where Go can apply it cheaply. Measured on the full 68006-file corpus: 41.41 s at 1 worker, 22.23 at 2, 10.65 at 4, 6.20 at 8, 5.28 at 16, 5.01 at 32 — a 7.8x speedup that flattens at the core count and gives almost nothing back after it, the same curve exec_oracle measured for php. Verdicts are identical to the serial oracle on all 68006 files. Default is GOMAXPROCS; TREEBANK_ORACLE_JOBS overrides it, the same knob exec_oracle uses.

grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.summary: tree-sitter-go accepts a superset of what go/parser accepts, in four measured ways. This is the same direction as tree-sitter-python's deliberate Python 2 support: the grammar accepts, the oracle rejects. It can never manufacture a sweep gap — a gap is 'grammar rejected AND oracle accepted' — so gap_files stays exact. What it does constrain is the negative corpus, which cannot contain any of these four.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.found_by: 24 hand-written invalid Go files, each confirmed rejected by go/parser, run against the grammar. 20 were correctly rejected and are now test/negative/. The 4 below were accepted.

cases.why: DELIBERATE UPSTREAM DESIGN, stated in grammar.js's source_file rule: 'Unlike a Go compiler, we accept statements at top-level to enable parsing of partial code snippets in documentation (see #63).' Not patched — an editor parsing a partial buffer is upstream's stated use case.
Same rule and the same deliberate decision: source_file is a repeat over top-level declarations.

cases.case: variadic parameter that is not last
cases.why: DELIBERATE AND TESTED UPSTREAM: test/corpus/declarations.txt's 'Function declarations' case asserts `func f(x ... int, y ... int)` parses. It is also spec-conformant — the Go spec's EBNF is `ParameterDecl = [ IdentifierList ] [ "..." ] Type`, which permits ... on any parameter; 'can only use ... with final parameter' is a check go/parser applies after the grammar. ATTEMPTED AND REVERTED: restricting parameter_list to a final-only variadic generates cleanly, holds the sweep at 68006/68006 and does make the grammar reject it — but it deletes an upstream corpus test case, for zero corpus benefit. Changing a tested upstream decision on no evidence is the drift GRAMMARS.md warns about, so it was reverted rather than shipped.

cases.case: opening brace on the line after the signature
cases.why: STRUCTURAL. Go inserts a semicolon at end of line when the last token is an identifier, a literal, or one of `break continue fallthrough return ++ -- ) ] }`, so `func f()` ends the declaration and the following block is orphaned — go/parser says so. Modelling that needs the LEXER to insert semicolons, and tree-sitter-go has no external scanner at all (newline is the plain regex /\n/ used as an optional terminator). Not fixable in grammar.js; it would be a scanner.c job and a large one.

grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.why_this_is_safe: All four are accepts-invalid, never rejects-valid, so none of them can inflate gap_files or send an agent after a phantom bug. The cost is stated plainly: the negative corpus cannot pin any of these four, so a future patch that made one of them WORSE would not be caught here. Two are upstream's deliberate design, one is spec-conformant and upstream-tested, and one needs an external scanner that does not exist.
